I booted this up expecting space pew-pew and blue aliens.
What I got was an emotional breakdown wrapped in 120 hours of galactic diplomacy and regret.

One moment you’re flirting with an alien scientist, the next you’re questioning the morality of synthetic life while your ship’s AI roasts you.

This trilogy didn’t just “tell a story”, it kidnapped my sleep schedule, replaced my personality with Paragon/Renegade choices, and made me emotionally attached to pixels in space suits.
I went in thinking “haha laser guns”, and came out giving TED-Talks about AI ethics and crying over people who don’t exist.

Still the best sci-fi story ever told and honestly, if you didn’t cry at least once, you probably sided with the Reapers.

For ever a Dragon Age & Mass Effect nerdy boy...

If there's anyone out there who still hasn't played the Mass Effect trilogy yet, I have two things for you: 

First thing is this collection should be a no brainer purchase. You get all 3 games and pretty much everything they have to offer. 

The second thing is I am extremely jealous that you get to experience this masterpiece of a trilogy for the first time.

[h3]First things first.[/h3]
If you already have all the Mass Effect games and their DLC, this version isn't super easy to recommend unless you're just a hyper-fan, such as myself. However, if you're a person that does [u]not[/u] possess all three games and their DLC in one place, I can highly recommend this version.

The mouse and keyboard controls for these games are subpar, truth be told. Especially for ME1 where it originally never told you that you can drag and drop abilities into the hotbar. These games were designed for consoles first. The original release dates span from 2007-2012. Designing games for console first was/is just how the Triple A industry functioned, especially at the time. We're seeing a slight shift away from that now and I suppose you could argue they should have changed how the game functions in this remaster, but I would contend that [u]this version is essentially a collection with improved visuals more than anything else. It's simply not a remake.[/u]

Beyond the basic graphics settings such as anti-aliasing and v-sync, there's almost nothing else. Even the brightness setting is buried in “calibration” rather than video settings. Luckily, the games are all pretty old and don't require much to run anymore. Though, for a remaster especially, it's disheartening to not even have things like an FOV slider. Ultrawide support works, but it's got black bars on the side during cutscenes — which, in my experience of using ultrawide for the past year and half, it's pretty common for “official 21:9 support” — but still very disheartening to not see it implemented properly.

Depending on which Mass Effect you ask me of, I've played them 3-5 times through, prior to this version. However, one thing I cannot truly comment on is the differences that importing a save can do. As I have never done it. Essentially every playthrough of each game was a brand new Shepard to me. I've played ME1 and ME2 mostly on X360, truth be told. It wasn't until ME3 that I started playing on PC. So from that aspect alone, this is version offers me something I've never actually seen.

[u]I won't talk much about the story[/u] — you're either like me, in that, you've already played these games multiple times or you're somewhere between never having gotten into them or possibly having never even heard of them. So it's a moot point of contention.

[h3]Mass Effect 1:[/h3]
[b]This is still the most important and [i]classic[/i] of the series.[/b]

But no worries, it's still very much ME1. You'll need to spec into specific weapon types to do real damage. It's most assuredly improved, in that, you won't miss someone two feet away if you're not leveled into the weapon type nor will the sniper rifle sway be so absurd—as if Shepard had never held a weapon before. But ME1 remains the most [i]traditional[/i] as far as RPG elements of all the games.

[b]Though, ME1 was not without faults[/b]:
One of the mains issues with ME1 can be seen in a similar design aspect from Dragon Age Inquisition, similarities include the intro being action packed, then followed by an extreme amount of exposition in a semi-convoluted map. Tedious tutorial quests posing as fetch-quests give little to no urgency to the main story. Essentially not telling the player that they could leave. (Citadel, Hinterlands)

The other issues I've always had is that in requiring you to perform paragon or renegade actions to earn more dialogue options disables you to be more neutral. Without the points, you're unable to choose certain dialogue later on making certain situations impossible to have a favorable outcome without prior knowledge and preparation.

[h3]ME1 to ME2 tonal-genre shift.[/h3]
Many purport Mass Effect 1 to be rather clunky — when what they mean to say is that it's not a great shooter. That's because ME1 was actually much closer to a traditional RPG. The way you spec'd a character and the party members you brought were paramount to success — putting points into specific weapons types increased your accuracy and damage. Having party members that either specialized in tech or biotics—the things that you didn't—mattered. Whereas ME2 and 3 are essentially action games, almost completely devoid of any role-playing aspects outside of dialogue choices.

There's less loot/inventory management in ME2 and 3. Combat is more strait-forward as well — they become relatively generic cover-shooters at this stage. [This is not inherently negative.] ME2 — armor/weapons/upgrades are either researched or purchased or you'll discover blueprints. Only skills are leveled into, no longer weapon types—dictated rather by [b]class[/b]. Which essentially boil down to three types: [b]Adept, Soldier and Engineer[/b]. Specialists in Biotics, Combat and Tech respectively. However, there are also what I call half n' half classes in [b]Vanguard[/b]—Biotic/Combat, [b]Sentinel[/b]— Tech/Biotic and finally [b]Infiltrator[/b]— Tech/Combat. These are persistent through the entire series.

Other things like cover being auto-entered in ME1—ME2 introduced vaulting and thermal clips—heavy ammo. The guns behave like traditional weapons that need to be reloaded. ME3 also introduces active-roll/dodge and a more robust melee system.

This genre shift is similar to what we observed in the Dragon Age series where the mechanics in Origins to DA2 was akin to something like Baldur's Gate turning into Diablo. Again, these are not inherently bad choices, I love me a good action game. But I've felt for a long time that when establishing a new IP, shifting their core mechanics in this slightly off-putting, if not pernicious way ended up taking away what made those games special in the first place. Turning a fervent niche into a drab, generic blockbuster hit for the masses. This focus-shift to action culminates in Andromeda.

[h3]Paragon/Renegade[/h3]  [b]It's no different from the originals, as far as I can tell. [/b]
[olist]
[*] ME1 uses a total points system earned by choices that then unlock the charm/intimidate stats that need to be leveled into to unlock other dialogue options.

[*] ME2 uses choices to change paragon/renegade percentage. Charm/Intimidate stat removed and replaced by the ability to interrupt dialogue instead.

[*] ME3 uses a reputation system that both paragon/renegade points go into.[/olist]

[h3]Misc:[/h3]
You're able to alter the appearance and class of [i]your[/i] Shepard, even if importing a save. You can also play differently as far as paragon/renegade—somewhere in the middle each game. The way you play has more immediate effects. However, the games feature many [i]major[/i] decisions that have far reaching — and often unforeseen — consequences going into the other games.

ME1 to ME2 hacking mini-game switches from circle frogger to timed variations of matching games. ME3 essentially has no mini-games instead focusing on “Total Military Strength” as a sort of meta-game. The original multiplayer part that went into this score is no longer used.

In ME1, the galaxy map is simply menu to be navigated. In ME2, there are no more sites to be landed on and explored with the Mako, instead you'll find anomalies that you'll shuttle down to. The galaxy map becomes more interactable. You directly control the ship's movements and this costs fuel. Resource gathering is then performed by scanning and sending probes down. ME3 focuses on scanning and obtaining War Assets.

[b]Note: This review won't be about the game or the story itself really- it's the same trilogy we fell in love with. Rather, this review is to primarily focus on the changes between the original games and the Legendary Edition.[/b]

[h1][u]Graphics:[/u][/h1]
The most obvious changes are the graphics, and wow does it stand out. In all three games, especially in Mass Effect 3 did it look very polished, detailed, and rendered beautifully. The lighting as well as the scenery stood out, more visually than before and the special effects as well as the atmosphere ... all in 4k. Characters also look polished and not as ugly anymore, though the models in Mass Effect 1 definitely aren't going to look as good as those in ME 2 & 3.

[h1][u]Photo Mode:[/u][/h1]
Surprisingly something we didn't ask for, but was much needed. Now it's very easy to pause the game whenever (even during combat) and just zoom in, rotate the camera, change filters, adjust the brightness or blur out the background to make the characters focused, ect. The amount of screenshots and pictures I took is insane, and a very welcome edition to this game. Trust me, go to Discord or Reddit devoted to Mass Effect, and the amount of pictures is staggering.

[h1][u]Controller Support:[/u][/h1]
Unlike the previous games on PC, they did not come with Controller Support. You would of had to install a program online or do specific steps in getting it to work with your controller, and even then it was a pain. Now you can just use an Xbox One controller or a PC controller without issue. As someone who grew up playing on console, this was a must have for me to enjoy the game more.

[h1][u]Changes:[/u][/h1]
While I didn't think they would do it, a number of things (appearances, design, events, ect) have been changed. I came across a few things they changed for the better, and one in particular is a spoiler in ME 3, but it was so good to see them change (involves Tali). The biggest changes are likely in ME 1, with environment changes and how the layout looks, along with the fact combat is more smooth and balanced in ME 1 now. In ME 2 & 3, it's unchanged for the most part, but the interface as well as quality of life improvements are there.

[h1][u]Problems:[/u][/h1]
I won't lie, despite I loved playing Legendary Edition, there was numerous problems I came across. One major issue stemmed from collision. In ME 1, 2, and 3, sometimes Shepard will find himself going over terrain or passing over into a wall, only to get stuck and nothing will fix that unless you restart a save or the mission itself. Another issue is the flare being incredibly bright at times, even toning it down to it's lowest, the flare and 'shine' of things can be blinding. Sometimes lip syncing is a bit off (ME 1 and ME 3 had a few instances of this) and followers not popping in at times. There is also no multiplayer which was a massive let down. I loved the multiplayer in ME 3, being able to play any race was so incredible and the wave of enemies per round was exciting to survive in with my friends. I wish they included it.

My biggest issue with all 3 games was the AI. At times, the enemy AI can be dumb to auto bot levels depending on the circumstances. I played on Insanity and ME 2 had every enemy become an auto bot, always aiming for me in a split second with 100% perfect accuracy and never aiming for anyone else, even walking PAST my allies to shoot me. Then you have my AI squadmates being very broken or dumb, depending on again, the circumstances. In ME 1, they were so useless it was painful. In ME 2, they were alright but had some dumb moments. In ME 3, they could carry me and I would look at my phone as they did all the work (if you build them right). Balance and AI are a big problem in Legendary, and I hope they improve AI for everyone's sanity.

[h1][u]Worth It?[/u][/h1]
Truth be told, if you want to relive the trilogy and have an excuse, I say go for it. The price is reasonable despite a lot of people want the game cheaper or free if they own the original games already. But if you think about it, all 3 games ($20 each) plus every DLC released are free in Legendary Edition. But apart from that, despite I did very much enjoy playing this trilogy all over again, the changes aren't that big in scope. Mostly just better graphics, better framerate, adjustments in combat and adding a few changes to scenes / design of things. If you're a huge fan like me and don't mind, then yea it is worth. But if you aren't that impressed with the perks of Legendary Edition, you aren't missing out on too much. Legendary Edition is like the old trilogy but in nicer paint, polished, and got some upgrades. But even with that said, this was such a treat and I enjoyed every moment, even with the stacked cons. Amazing series overall, a must have whether it's the older games or Legendary Edition.

[h1] My Life has No Purpose Now [/h1]

To start off, I have never played a Mass Effect title before this. I've been aware of the series for a long time but the trilogy was never really on my radar. With the release of the Legendary Edition, I decided that I'd give it a go. After completing all 3 games and their DLC after over 147 hours, all I have to say is that I'm more than glad to have had this experience!

[b] The Story [/b]
The story is amazing and intriguing. The world building does a great job creating the setting of the games where there is conflict between the different species that leads to the point of where the first game starts. What makes the story great is throughout the games, the player is presented with many situations that don't just have a straight forward answer. Instead, it creates a grey area that really makes you think about the choice you're about to make and how it will impact the story later. It's hard to believe that the story is nearly a decade old. That just goes to show how timeless the games are. 

[b] The Characters [/b]
What makes the Mass Effect Trilogy special and what enhances the story are the squadmates. Each of them are unique with their own backstories, flaws, and how they can interact with Shepard. There are some who aren't as good as others [spoiler] *cough cough Jacob cough cough* [/spoiler], but otherwise, the characters are the best part of the games. The more Shepard talks to everyone, the more he/she learns about them. Because of this, there are characters that I will admit I didn't think I would like as much as I do. That just shows how well the characters are written! Some of my favorite characters include Garrus, Tali, Liara, Thane, and Mordin. 

[b] Mass Effect 3's Ending [/b]
I feel like this needs to addressed so I'll keep it brief without going into spoiler territory. Before playing, I heard that the ending of the trilogy is bad and unfulfilling due to choices not effecting it and a few other reasons. This was one of the things that originally deterred me from playing. After seeing the ending myself, I can say that I feel that the ending isn't super terrible but doesn't give closure to everything that happens in the game, ESPECIALLY in relation to what happens to the squadmates we all grew to love. Overall, not the highlight of the trilogy. 

[b] Conclusion [/b]
Overall, I really loved my time playing the trilogy for the first time. Even through the ending isn't the best, it isn't what makes the trilogy special, it's the experience of playing them and interacting with your squadmates! Now that I've finished the story in its entirety, I feel sad now knowing that I'll never experience it again for the first time and that there likely will never be a trilogy like this again. There are many other great games out there but the Mass Effect Trilogy is an experience of its own. I can now say with confidence that the Mass Effect Trilogy is now among my favorite games of all time!

Science fiction role-playing game in which, as Commander Shepard, you make decisions that affect the fate of the galaxy and the development of the story.

After more than 130 hours of Commander Shepard's beautiful adventure, I finished this great game and I regret that there are fewer and fewer  games like this, where you can follow the adventure of one character for over 130 hours with practically the same team. I fell in love with Commander Shepard and the whole team.                                                       [h1] GENERAL ADVANTAGES [/h1]

It's worth not skipping them, as some of the dialogues are epic and very funny
✅As for the game world, it's really huge in each of these parts of the game, and I have great respect for the developers for managing to do it (from places truly teeming with life to dark places of horror)

The Mass Effect trilogy is one of gaming's greatest triumphs. It was a product of BioWare's golden age of imagination and creativity. Not only that it changed the way people perceive the action RPG genre, but video games in general.

It's an extraordinary journey that spans multiple years in this universe full of danger and mystery, but also hope and compassion. The lore and writing is so brilliantly presented and thought-out. That you end up experiencing the consequences in the third game because of your actions in the first. No wonder it's so easy to immerse yourself and dive right in.

No doubt the game's greatest virtue lies in it's strong narrative and player choice. At first your decisions are small in comparison to what's to come. But over time the game escalates things beautifully. Everything from deciding who you are, and who will you become. To the fate of the entire world being placed in your hands.

Each new game improves upon the last with better visuals, snappier combat, grander scale of events, more interesting companions, sleeker gameplay and of course, even more decisions for the player to make. And the impact of your choices can be observed throughout the entire playthrough. Entire civilizations can be saved or lost, innumerable amount of essential characters can survive or perish, romances can thrive or wither. The amount of things that can change from playthrough to playthrough is staggering.

The first Mass Effect introduces Shepard. The second game challenges the protagonist's beliefs and integrity. And the third game humanizes Shepard. Most of the choices that you end up making, will not only change the world around you, but also change you too. Will you inspire people through love or fear ? Will you be charming or intimidating ? Some of my favorite trilogy moments stem from Shepard's inspirational and compelling speeches. But it's not just Shepard that changes, his entire entourage of both familiar and alien allies changes too.

There's so many great characters throughout the trilogy, so much potential. Understanding how they think, talking to them in-between missions and figuring out what makes them tick was always one of my favorite things to do in Mass Effect. You will no doubt end up having favorites, and that's normal! Eventually you will start feeling a real connection and sympathy for at least one of your allies. Whether it will be towards someone who is seeking absolution. Or someone who is searching for a home, or a family. Or just someone who is looking for a big ugly monster to beat the crap out of. "Who am I?" is a question that resonated strongly with me in particular. Legion, EDI and even Shepard are all faced with this question. And you as a player have the ability to directly influence all of it.

It's the characters that are the lifeblood and core of Mass Effect. Forging long-lasting relationships is key. Your allies will often reference things that you did for them in previous games or quote something that you might have said. They will be there for you as you have been for them. Even the villains are likeable and compelling to me.

Some of the most common themes or recurring leitmotifs are: loyalty, belonging, self-sacrifice and peace. Your role in this universe is much bigger than it seems at first. You go from saving a tiny colony, to saving a planet, to saving an entire solar system, to saving the galaxy and deciding the fate of every living thing in it. But the universe demands balance. And every decision for something is a decision against something else.

Now for some technical bits before I wrap this up. For a trilogy released a decade ago, it still looks and performs great. Yes, the remaster enhances the textures and meshes and adds extra post-processing. But the aesthetics and overall sci-fi look of the game remains the same. The set pieces are unique, very different from planet to planet and memorable in their own way. Speaking of mods, I recommend using a couple to address the busy work, such as: instant planet probing, skipping hacking minigames, infinite galaxy map scanning. With that out of the way, how do I feel about the actual games themselves? All I can say is it's been legendary. I've been a massive fan of the series since 2012 and revisiting it after ten years has been incredibly exciting, emotional, and rewarding. Each game has its many strengths and weaknesses, but the one trait all of them share is unbridled passion and creativity. Each fully deserving of their own review but for the sake of time and real estate, an insightful but quick analysis will have to do. 

[h1] Mass Effect [/h1]

The first Mass Effect used to be the black sheep of the family. It was referred to by many as the gatekeeper of the series and with good reasons. Despite its strong story and characters, the clunky gameplay and rapidly aging graphics were becoming increasingly evident as the generation progresses. However, that's no longer the case with the Legendary Edition. With mods, I had the time of my life with this game. With all of the rough edges polished, the excellent plot, likable characters, and amazing lore were able to shine through like never before seen. To my absolute shock and delight, It went from being my least favorite to my second favorite game in the series, and the only reason it didn't take that top spot is because of the game I'm going to talk about next.  

[h1] Mass Effect 2 [/h1]

Otherwise known as the Crème de la crème of the series, it should come as no surprise to anyone that Mass Effect 2 is my favorite game out of the three, and so often the case with many others, and one only has to play a few hours to begin to understand why so many fans hold it in such high regard. A simple but effective plot gives us a strong goal to work toward, an incredibly memorable and well-written cast of characters, a darker and seedier approach to the tone of the galaxy, the enigmatic and charismatic Illusive Man played flawlessly by Martin Sheen, a more refined and streamlined approach to the gameplay, and what you have in the end is a game that epitomizes everything of what a true sequel should be. Whatever weaknesses it has is profoundly outweighed by the positives, and ten years later I'm thrilled to say that Mass Effect 2 is still one of my favorite games of all time. 

[h1] Mass Effect 3 [/h1]

Where do I begin with this game? On one hand, it has some of the best writing and iconic moments in the entire series. And on the other, some of the most nonsensical, insulting, and downright baffling writing and design choices I've ever seen. One moment you want to sing to the choir about how good the game is, and the next you wonder whether the writing team collectively suffered a massive stroke and were forced to hire chimpanzees to complete the story halfway through. In all seriousness, Mass Effect 3 is the product of a team who worked themselves tirelessly to the brink of physical and mental exhaustion, in states which I can only assume are akin to sweatshop-like conditions, and forced to meet impossible and unrealistic deadlines by Electronic Arts. Not only was Bioware trying to create one of the most ambitious RPGs ever made, but they also had to do it in significantly less time than any of their previous two games, while simultaneously developing a tacked-on multiplayer horde mode. So, as much as I want to scold them for doing such a half-a$$ job with what was supposed to be their magnum opus, I can't help but developed an immense sense of respect and gratitude that the game came out as competently as it did. If you can't tell by now, I'm emotionally torn on this game. [u] I truly do love it [/u] and see the potential in it, but I can't help but feel a sense of disappointment and regret every time I play the game knowing how different and extraordinary it could've been had things turned out differently. If I can leave a piece of advice for anyone going into Mass Effect 3, it's this: Enjoy the game for what it is because there is a lot to love about it. The highs are amazingly high, but prepare yourself for the lows because that sh!t will be lower than the Mariana Trench. 

[h1] Parting Words [/h1]

Despite its shaky and questionable finale, the Mass Effect trilogy had a profound impact on me as it did on so many others. Playing again ten years later, it reminds me why the series was so beloved and had rightly earned such legendary status among fans. Its breathtaking worldbuilding and lore, well-told story, and diverse and well-written ensemble of characters have forever etched themselves into the annals of gaming history. It truly was, and still is, the most epic sci-fi video game saga of all time. And that is why Mass Effect Legendary Edition is my favorite game on the Citadel. I should go.

Having played the original trilogy when it first released almost 20 years ago, I had forgotten just how great this series is. Filled with amazing imagery, solid writing / voice acting and immersive gameplay that really makes you feel like a badass flying through space saving the galaxy. For me it feels a bit like a spiritual successor to the Knights of the Old Republic games in many ways, tying space sim elements to a story-deep action RPG. As the series progresses, so does the quality of life changes and positive changes to some of the weaker elements of the first game. Visually, the whole thing is stunning and still manages to hold up today - though I would recommend installing a couple of mods just to make your experience that much greater. I used the ALOT and ALOV mods which feature upscaled textures and videos. 

For those completely new to the series, essentially this is a third person action RPG, using a cover system. The game tends to split between exploration, gunplay and the story-driven narrative, employing a morality system that lets you determine what kind of galactic saviour you are. You might be a paragon of hope, making decisions to be kind and benevolent, or a renegade who takes any action available to them to get the job done. Of course, many difficult decisions are present in this series, ones that will certainly carry over even from the first game to the third. That renegade decision might ultimately be the right move for example - or it might just be funny or cool! 

The first game of this series released in 2007 - and it mostly holds up very well. That said, some of the controls and gunplay feel a little restrictive, and I would have liked to see more features such as FOV control or shoulder cam switching. That said, the second game vastly improves on the shooting elements. The other thing I feel I should mention is the awful EA launcher that tries forcing you to launch after you install. I highly recommend looking up the 'F@@@ EA guide' which gives you a very useful way of avoiding it altogether. Of course, there was some controversy with how the last game ended back in the day, and this ended up with a lot of drama unfortunately. Without giving too many spoilers regarding that, I'll just say the ending felt quite rushed. There are a lot of mods and a patch that Bioware released, though I never tried it myself as this is the first time I've replayed the series since completing it all those years ago. 

On a final note, as anyone who is a fan of Star Trek or similar, RPGs or Sci-Fi stories, this collection is a must-have, and probably for me one of the best game series of all time.

[b]Recommended mods:[/b]
For the entire trilogy, I recommend ALOT (Texture improvements), ALOV (AI upscaled videos) and Lighting Restoration. These mods are available for each game as packs and make a lot of improvements that bring the ME series almost to the current gen in a lot of ways. 

To vastly improve the ending of ME3, I highly, highly recommend getting CEM (Citadel Epilogue Mod). This basically places one of ME3s DLCs at the end of the game, which basically acts as a heart warming goodbye to all the characters in the game. It just fits so well, especially since the DLC contrasted with the grim narrative of the final game.

Lastly, for ME3, make sure to get EGM (Expanded Galaxy Mod). This adds a huge bunch of new quests and truly difficult decisions that effect your final army for the last fight, in a totally meaningful way. It adds so much more immersion to the game - I mean a LOT. The maker of the mod deserves so much credit. There is one scene that allows you to call in the final battle near the end of the game that is genuinely one of the most kino moments in gaming I've experienced.

This review started as just pointing out the most noticeable changes in the Legendary Edition compared to the original editions, then it transformed into regular reviews of each game, and ended with a rant about ME3. A stream of consciousness kind of a review, if you will.

The promised United Character Creation, isn't. After importing my Shepard from ME1 to ME2 I discovered that his eyebrows and stubble were missing and his skin became pasty white i.e. he looked sickly AF. Had to re-enter his ID code in Custom Appearance menu to be able to modify him. Should have been a separate option without needing to do so. From ME2 to ME3 his hair and skin were fine, but his eyes became much larger. I checked - it's the same set of eyes, they are just bigger in ME3. Weird.

ME1: Finished in 28 hours on Hardcore. Always liked it for essentially being the middle market AA game, compared to the rest of the series. The planet exploration element, along with the Mako, were some of my favorite moments, despite the overwhelming jankiness.
The most noticeable improvements:[list]
[*]High resolution textures, better looking assets (taken from later games) and improved lighting which makes the game look newer by about ~5 years. Noveria's Port Hanshan doesn't look as bland anymore. It is a bit too dark at times though, especially Feros.
[*]The men do not look like crap for no reason and are more in line with the women.
[*]Unlocked FPS, which was locked to 30 in the older PC port.
[*]Very sleek and compact looking HUD.
[*]Many talent and weapon balance changes, headshots have been added.
[*]Achievement balance changes e.g. the "spend an arbitrary amount of time with specific squadmate" was just changed to a simple "complete 5 missions with X in your team". This makes it possible to unlock all ME1 achievements in a single playthrough.[/list]
Had a few minor bugs. Twice the Mako got permanently stuck on a mountain on some uncharted world and I had to return to the Normandy. Twice it got temporarily stuck (~10 seconds) on Noveria. No crashes. Easily much better PC version than the original and overall much less janky.

ME2: Finished in 34 hours on Hardcore. The moment where Mass Effect went from hard sci-fi middle market game to a space opera blockbuster AAA game. I still don't know why they decided to kill Shepard and then instantly resurrect him/her. You would think this kind of drastic measures are taken when the writer paints themselves into a corner. 
However, the gameplay upgrade is impressive (aside from the streamlining of gear upgrades and inventory management). Each class has now a distinct ability, which makes them unique compared to the others. The person who came up with the Vanguard Charge must have had a true revelation: it's arguably the best addition to the series as a whole. And then there's the scanning minigame, which is just a mistake of nature. The hacking minigames are an improvement though.
The soundtrack was great in ME1, but in ME2 it's even better, especially in the DLCs; often epic and grandiose. The hubs are much smaller than the Citadel from ME1, but each of them is distinct and presents some breathtaking landscapes. The ambient in clubs such as Afterlife is still impressive a decade since release.
The most noticeable improvements:[list]
[*]Better textures and lighting, but it's not as noticeable as it is in ME1.
[*]All the DLC weapon and armor packs are neatly integrated into the game. You have to buy or research them. The stronger gear can only be obtained later on e.g., Kestrel Armor, arguably the best armor in ME2, is available on Illium.
[*]More ammo. It was way too scarce, especially when using sniper rifles.[/list]
I've seen some minor visual issues like NPCs snapping into place during cutscenes or enemies behaving weirdly; it might have to do with the FPS being unlocked, not sure though. Twice the game froze on a black screen after selecting squadmates during the Suicide Mission. I had to kill the process. I think I did it too fast and doing it a bit slower is the workaround. No crashes.

ME3: Finished in 35 hours on Hardcore. ME3 was rushed back in 2012: the UI (which looks a bit placeholder-y at times) was not scaled for PCs like ME2 and there are large windows with gigantic fonts clearly made for TVs, some of the animations are just bad or broken (e.g. the "activating ammo power" animation which worked perfectly fine in ME2), the hacking minigames were removed altogether, and the only hub in the game is the Citadel which is separated into small floors. There is also a ton of "listen to NPC and find arbitrary item somewhere in the game world" quests taken straight from Dragon Age 2. A clear sign of not enough time.
However, the combat is much faster than in the previous installments: movement in and out of cover is much quicker, sprinting is infinite, cooldowns are shorter, and you can dodge. Weapon modding and upgrading were reintroduced, as well as weight was added which influences length of cooldowns. 
Furthermore, while walking around the Citadel you are no longer in armor and your squadmates are using their shore leave by themselves instead of following you everywhere; they also communicate with each other on the Normandy. 
There's this sense of desperation within the entire game, especially seen in e.g. refugee camps on the Citadel. It's well contrasted with the often humorous camaraderie: between Shepard and his squadmates it's amped up to 11, paving the way for some of the best fan service ever written in video games, and that's not counting Citadel DLC.
Despite all my rambling, it is a good game: it has some strong writing, like Tuchanka or Rannoch arcs… but then you have a lot of auto-dialogue from Shepard and generally much fewer dialogue choices throughout; Cerberus being everywhere and as powerful as the Empire from Star Wars for no reason; Kai Leng, an anti-Shepard, being only fleshed out in the novels i.e. if you never read them, tough luck, you don’t even know who he is.
Do not get me started on the original ending. There’s a multitude of articles, hour long YouTube videos, and forum posts of epic proportions, all disseminating what was wrong with it. I can only add that it disappointed me so greatly, that I returned to Mass Effect, as a franchise, only now thanks to the Legendary Edition. To put it bluntly, the original ending was so bad, that I did not play any Mass Effect game for nearly a decade (not counting the ME3 multiplayer). It was not about having each and every decision reflected in the ending: I knew that was literally impossible to develop. It was about having closure and the ending being satisfying. I received none of those. The Extended Cut is infinitely better, as it does provide some closure, but it still is rather nonsensical given the themes throughout the series and even ME3 itself. Leviathan also adds some context to it, along with more dialogue options in the ending. I will end it here.

Citadel DLC is fantastic... but it should really be called The Apology DLC, because this is what it actually is. The ending soured so many, that only 3 metric tons of fan service could sweeten it up. Sad.

Overall, ME LE is worth it, though I had hoped they would have fixed ME3’s technical issues, just as they did in ME1. At this point it’s more janky than ME1.

The best RPG game.
And the more time you spend with it, the less you want to compare it to anything else.
Mass Effect isn’t about builds or numbers. It’s about decisions you make when there’s no reload button for your conscience. About characters you get attached to without even noticing. About moments that stay with you long after the credits roll.
Legendary Edition is the best way to experience this story as a whole. From your first steps on the Citadel to the final choice that no longer feels like just a “game choice.”
After thousands of hours, one thing became clear: people don’t come back here for gameplay alone. They come back for the feeling that you were part of something bigger. That you had a crew. A team. People who mattered.
Finishing the perfect ending leaves a strange kind of emptiness. Not because there’s nothing left to do, but because the story is truly over. And you don’t really want to let it go.
If you’re still wondering whether it’s worth starting — the answer is obvious.
It is.And if you’ve already played it — you know exactly why you’ll return.
One thing that really hits differently in MELE is how it balances the fate of the galaxy with the fate of people. You’re not just a soldier running from one explosion to another — you’re someone carrying the weight of impossible choices that ripple through entire civilizations, but also through friendships, romances, and personal struggles. That mix of epic and intimate never gets old.
The way each decision impacts not just the big picture but also the squad’s chemistry adds layers to the experience. You get to know these characters not as sidekicks, but as real people with their own fears, hopes, and flaws. That’s what makes replaying the trilogy so addictive — the story doesn’t just change, it feels alive because your connections change.
And the gameplay? It’s smooth enough to keep you hooked but deep enough to reward tactical thinking. MELE isn’t about flashy combos or endless button mashing; it’s about smart use of your squad’s skills and environment. Plus, the remaster cleaned up most rough edges, so it feels fresh without losing its soul. In the end, MELE isn’t just a game or even a series. It’s a living story that keeps pulling you back — not because it shouts the loudest, but because it whispers truths about sacrifice, loyalty, and what it means to fight for something bigger than yourself.

I've played through the Mass Effect trilogy three times, all on insanity. Two playthroughs as an Infiltrator (including my LE playthrough) and once as a vanguard.

MELE is a really good deal. One of the most distinctive aspects of the Mass Effect trilogy is that your decisions carry over between games, affecting entire storylines in substantial, sometimes joyous, sometimes tragic ways. Although the quality of the writing (most notably, the ending sequence of ME3, or the Jacob romance. If you know, you know) is not always perfect, I absolutely respect the sheer commitment to such an ambitious and epic scope. As a result of this design choice, the best experience for the Mass Effect trilogy is to play all three games, in order.

With this in mind, the single biggest barrier to playing the Mass Effect trilogy was playing through Mass Effect 1. Many of the design choices originally made in ME1 very clearly demonstrate the ways in which it is a shooter *designed by people who don't normally play shooters.* The result was that while ME1 was an excellent roleplaying experience, as a shooter it was clunky and frustrating to play.

MELE adds some gentle but important fixes to ME1 that make it much more playable, making the trilogy much easier to jump into. They removed the awkward, drunken shaking of the original sniper accuracy mechanic (you'd think a decorated soldier like Shepard knows how to HOLD A GUN) and replaced it with mild bullet spread (much more acceptable). They removed the bizarre XP penalty on killing units from inside the Mako (back in my day, we'd whittle things down to the last nub of HP, hop out of the mako, snipe it, then hop back in, to get full XP. Being able to stay in the Mako makes vehicle segments much more enjoyable). They changed the UI and brought it in line with ME2/ME3 UI (it used to be that your health bar was a tiny series of bars in the corner of your screen that you could barely see in-combat). And the addition of a horizontal booster and the reduction of the Mako's bounciness makes Mako exploration segments much nicer (that little boost to get over the top of a hill is so, so nice).

Aside from the improvements to ME1, having all of the DLCs included makes MELE a much richer experience than the original trilogy without DLCs was. In particular, the Mass Effect 2 DLCs Arrival and Lair of the Shadow Broker are, frankly, key parts of the trilogy, in that they serve as an important bridge between ME2 and ME3.

As a final parting note, Femshep x Liara forever!

TL;DR: They're almost the exact same as they were previously, just with some graphical overhauls and minor adjustments. All bugs, glitches, and exploits remain intact, while they sneakily added some of their own bugs and glitches along the way. It's a buggier experience than the original games, but not in a way that's going to hinder your love of the groundbreaking trilogy.

The Mass Effect Trilogy has a permanent place in my heart. The first game's RPG elements and open world concept that allows you to explore and implores you to learn more about the world that's carefully sculpted within. The second game's companions and worldbuilding that allows you to more learn more in-depth about the various alien cultures. The third game's emotional weight that only progressively gets heavier and heavier.

The Mass Effect Legendary Edition is what I'd call a soft-remaster. Most of what has been done is graphical overhauls, some of which are arguably for the better and others arguably for the worst. Some very minor gameplay changes were made and the user interface got a redesign that's more in line with the future installments of the series that are notably more shooter than RPG.

Pretty much every bug, exploit, and glitch are still in every one of the games. Hell, it seems like they added a few of their own, too. The Legendary Edition has proved to be buggier than the original games, whether it be Shepard's strange head movements in ME2 or enemies falling over and deciding not to move. They aren't necessarily gamebreaking, although on a couple of instances, enemies were knocked off the map and the game wouldn't progress and I was forced to reload.

There were some issues I had hoped they would resolve, such as ME1 being unable to hit Level 60 (or 30 depending on what level method you chose) without some sort of experience exploit, even if you kill every enemy, hack every container, and grab every collectible. By the end, I was still level 57 (or level 29) even on a true 100% run.

Many of the changes in the trilogy are questionable. Some ME2 character models are changed to be more in line with their ME3 counterparts, which ends up making them look really out of place (most notably Kelly Chambers), the Hammerhead in ME2 having its resource collection sound replaced with a god awful grinding sound that grates on your ears every time you use it, and if you saved the Council, Miranda doesn't mention it in the opening for ME2 anymore, instead replacing her "Shepard did everything right. Saving the Citadel -- even saving the Council" line with "Shepard uncovered the truth." They even replaced the gratuitous butt scenes from Miranda which sparked controversy despite the fact that Miranda's entire personality in ME2 is based on her being created to be "genetically perfect" and taking pride in her physique, which meant that the shots made sense for her character. Removing them isn't a big deal by any means, but it feels silly that they felt like they needed to remove them.

Still, some changes were welcome. The Mako in ME1 gaining a forward thrust helped resolve some of the issues players often had with it, and you are able to equip the ME3 casual outfits in ME2, which is great since the ME2 casual outfits weren't that great. Because of the saves being local to each other, Miranda no longer asks who the new Human Councilor is between Udina or Anderson, the game just recognizes your choice now. The ending for ME3 also includes more shots, expanding it ever so slightly in terms of what the player is shown.

Regardless of what I think of the changes, the Mass Effect Trilogy remains one of the best science fiction games to exist and the Legendary Edition IS the definitive way to experience all three games. Each game remains a fully independent beast with its own share of pros and cons, but the Legendary Edition unifies the games in a way that strings them into one cohesive experience rather than three "product of their time" games.

[h1]The Reality and the Legend[/h1] 

The Mass Effect Legendary Edition includes all three original Mass Effect games packaged together and remastered for contemporary and returning players. As such, the effectiveness of a review is diminished since each game is somewhat different, in both gameplay and presentation. Fortunately, there exist enough similarities and a congruent story arc, which make carrying out the task somewhat workable.  

The Legendary Edition generates an adequate platform to craft a supposition on what the trilogy achieved. The positive and the negative. With it being over nine years since the original release of the series’ final entry, this (nearly) all-encompassing Mass Effect package grants hindsight and a cooling-off period sufficient to reexamine what worked. And, conversely, what did not. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2685895008  

Each series’ entry does something better or worse than another game. There is no one-size-fits-all version of Mass Effect; mileage varies. And there are a lot of reasons for that. I have played through the entire series many times, and my favorite game, or the subjective “best” game, has been a title held by all of them. At their core, they are eloquent third-person RPG/shooters. But much of how they work is dependent upon the player’s playstyle, difficulty setting, and which of the three games is booted up. 

[h1]An Inciting Incident[/h1] 

Mass Effect 1, aside from being a shooter, prioritizes RPG elements in the form of an excellent story and novel planetary exploration. The narrative centers around a human player-character named Shepard, who is inevitably tasked with saving the galaxy from an ancient race of aliens known as “The Reapers.” The latter part is important too. As someone who enjoys sci-fi, the surveying of planets via a rover, “Mako,” is appealing. Exploration is limited, of course—after all, the game was originally released in 2007. But it still layers an identifiable tenet that is missing in the others. Chiefly, Mass Effect 1 tampered with the idea of traversing the heavens. Mass Effect 2 and 3 were only interested in them in as far as they could supply another combat arena or story beat.  

Using the Mako to travel empty swaths of planetary topography was received negatively, which created an overcorrection point for the series. Driving the Mako was mechanically clunky, and often there really wasn’t any place to drive to that couldn’t have just been portrayed in a cut scene. So, it was abandoned. Which is a shame, because while it rarely worked particularly well, it still dared to tackle the intimacy of visiting other worlds. Which is what the actual point of it was. Not driving a space car. 

Mass Effect 2 (and later, 3) shrunk in idealistic scope. Setting and plot stepped aside for characterization and spectacle. That is not to say the games diminished in content; Mass Effect 2 and 3 are, by all measures, bigger games. Rather, Bioware simply traded a smaller number of larger concepts for an abundance of increasingly safer, more conventional methods—like shooting things.  

[h1]Conflict and Characters[/h1] 

Mass Effect 2 continues (or pauses) the narrative from Mass Effect. The player-character is once again battling to stop the Reaper threat. But before doing so, Shepard must assemble a team of humans and aliens that each have a specific, and lethal, character trait that makes their participation vital. While lacking in narrative finesse, and never entirely shaking the feeling of being condensed, Mass Effect 2 is nevertheless more than equal to the task in other areas. For instance, it produced one of the greatest casts of party members in the history of its genre, something that the game’s overall structure needed. Each character is wholly unique, creating genuine catharsis and pathos as their stories flesh out. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2685893008   

Mass Effect 2 keeps things simple: you recruit a squad member, you get to know them, you earn their loyalty (via traditional corridor shooting scenarios), and you bring them to the final mission. There exist 12 recruits and each has a unique backstory, but the formula doesn't change. It is 12 times 2. Rinse, repeat. Onwards and upwards. Which means, narratively speaking, the characters must be excellent. As discussed, Mass Effect 2 achieved that end. 

Despite being a model of video game characterization, the narrative timeout and recruiting of a (mostly) new squad does funny things to the overall Mass Effect arc. Mass Effect 2 is, essentially, a soft reboot. Its end goal is stated very early in the game, and despite a few surprises, it never deviates from that path. You have a mission. You recruit your team. You complete the mission. 

It does layer on narrative freedom in the form of returning binary choices from the original (“renegade” and “paragon” selections) to carry over to the finale. But aside from that, it simply delays the inevitable end state coming in Mass Effect 3. And introduces a new, less sympathetic villain.  

Taken on its own, it might be the best Mass Effect. Taken as part of the whole, it might be the worst.  

[h1]Climax and Falling Action[/h1] 

Finally, there’s Mass Effect 3, a game whose reputation usually won’t extend past a dissenting discussion of its ending. But Mass Effect 3 still manages to do a lot of things right. Gameplay is at its most robust here. Transitioning from shooting an enemy, throwing a power at another, using your squad to launch supporting attacks, and so on, is excellent. The number of selectable team members is reduced from Mass Effect 2, but that’s perfectly natural—stories tend to contract as they move toward a finale. And for all its negative press, Mass Effect 3 still did an excellent job of building toward a conclusion. The story teems with sentiment, melancholy, and, as it nears its ending, dread.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2685896537  

The entire trilogy is based on the illusion of choice. The player is prompted to make several selections that feign major consequences for story beats that usually never come. Really, players have more micro influence than macro. The sheer dissonance from what consumers felt entitled to experience and what came to fruition in the ending was massive. And as a result, the conclusion felt lacking and meaningless. 

It is not without great irony that so much of Mass Effect’s storyline is about battling the insignificance of existence. Our collective resistance to being forgotten after we die is an inescapable part of the human experience after all. And that is what Mass Effect is [I]really[/i] about: struggling against our own irrelevance. And that’s a helluva thesis to punctuate satisfyingly.  

So, it’s no wonder the ending failed. 

But I still cannot resist drawing parallels between what the story was about and what the ending lacked: meaning, context, reason.  

Did my choices matter? Well... do they ever? 

[h1]Denouement[/h1] 

Mass Effect is special. The first part for its storytelling, the sequel for its characters, and the finale for all the best and worst attributes of the whole. It is flawed, but by focusing on its issues, it’s easy to ignore its accomplishments. Few video games put together a story on this scale so cohesively. And that’s what makes its shortcomings occasionally so devastating. 

For my part, I love the trilogy, and the Legendary Edition exists as the best articulation of it. The contents of the package present one of the finer video game arcs of its generation. If you have never, you should. And if you did, you might rediscover it again.  

Perhaps, without hype and spin, the experience will prove altogether changed.

It's very difficult for me to speak in a reasonable manner about the Mass Effect trilogy because of my undying love for it.

Replaying Mass Effect is like visiting old friends from your college years. You haven't seen them in years, you've probably been lax at keeping in touch via social media. You've grown as a person—perhaps drastically. Maybe your life situation has changed as well; you're working a lot, you've gotten married, you've had kids. Yet the moment you enter the same room as your old friends, you fall immediately into common ground. You're laughing at the same old things, sharing inside jokes once again. It may have been years (nearly 15, in Mass Effect's case) since you first met each other, but the moment you spoke once more, it's like you've never left. Garrus makes a calibration joke and you laugh the same way you always have. Wrex smashes something and you chuckle. Mordin sings. Jacob says something boring. In these moments you forget that these are video game characters and that you've already seen these scenes—perhaps dozens of times before. They are real people to us, and they are capable of affecting our lives the way real people do, despite them being aliens in a schlocky space opera.

This is the impact that Mass Effect's characters have on players. There are thousands of stories out there from people who were ill, or considered themselves depressed, or perhaps were even near suicide—all of whom exhibit undying love for this series because these games gave them succor they desperately needed at hard times in their lives. Such is the power of well-written fiction, and Mass Effect succeeds in spades in that regard. Its worldbuilding and character writing are second to none in the medium of gaming. It confronts us with people who feel real and allows us to take agency on their behalf, to try and make their lives a little better. It shows us a world not unlike our own, with its prejudices and its flaws, and gives us the power that we lack in real life to affect change regarding these issues in the fiction. It allows us to become better people in real life by examining serious issues such as bigotry, state corruption, greed, cruelty, and the cost of due process. We see these issues through the eyes of another and decide what our player character might do to right such wrongs. As always, fiction is the great lie through which we tell the truth, and if Mass Effect doesn't cultivate a little empathy in your blackened, shriveled gamer-soul, then nothing will.

But, enough waxing poetic. I know you're all, "Shut up, Jon Umber, you bag of hot wind! Everyone already knows how great the Mass Effect trilogy is. How does it run!?"

The answer to this, so far, is mixed, but I definitely believe this is a far superior version to the original PC port. On my setup I'm holding 100+ fps at full 4k with relative ease. This is a big deal, as the original games were limited to 62 fps thanks to the way they used physics, so the unlocked framerate is a massive plus here. The higher resolution textures look fantastic, and the new lighting and screen space reflections are really something. I expect we'll see some great photos being shared via the game's new Photo Mode relatively soon. The only drawback to the visual improvements that I've noticed so far is the characters seem to get a bit bug-eyed at times. I think this was due to the original game having much harsher, darker shadows, and perhaps covering up some character model issues specifically with the eyes. The animation has also aged notably, especially with the advent of performance capture technology in modern games, so expect some wooden facial animations and unnatural lip syncing, despite the effort made to remaster these games. All three games lack a field of view slider, which is a big negative for me. It's desperately needed since the camera is quite claustrophobic when your gun is drawn. In addition to this, I experience regular, debilitating framerate stuttering when traversing planets in the Mako in Mass Effect. I'm not sure what's causing this, but my framerate (which is typically locked at 100+) varies wildly from 55 to 75 fps in these instances. Fiddling with graphical settings has not alleviated the issue. I assume it's a texture streaming issue, due to the new high-res textures added to the game. Additionally, I have seen some people complaining about mouse acceleration, but the mouse action feels fine to me. Your mileage may vary.

Ultimately, this is very far from what I'd call a great PC port. However, the original PC ports of these games were absolutely awful, and Legendary Edition is clearly superior to those, even with its lack of graphics options and tendency to stutter. It looks fantastic when compared to the originals. If you played the original game or have a high tolerance for older games, you'll love Legendary Edition's changes. The best remasters make old games look like they do in your rose-tinted memory, and Legendary Edition accomplishes that in spades.

The gameplay changes are rather minor in the latter two games, but even in the first Mass Effect—the game which received the most attention—they are not groundbreaking. I noticed that Insanity feels markedly easier, so I think there's been some balancing done to level out some of the absurd difficulty spikes in the original game. One change I don't care for is that sniper rifles are now easily usable by all classes. I think this is a bit unbalanced and removes a lot of the value of the Infiltrator class, specifically, but I understand why they did it: It doesn't really make sense to pull out a rifle and suddenly begin aiming like a drunk person with Parkinson's. The Mako is still rather wonky, but the added stickiness does make it feel better. There are also some noteworthy changes to boss fights, but I won't spoil those. Suffice it to say they're all excellent, and bring some much-needed freshness to the significant encounters of the game. Ultimately the changes are quite minor; enough to feel like a marked improvement over the original game, but not so much that they alter the core experience of the games. BioWare did a phenomenal job toeing this line. It couldn't have been easy to do, but they nailed it.

The Mass Effect trilogy is an incredible experience, and this is by far the best way to play it, even when considering the great texture mods available for the original games. If you love the original trilogy and are considering Legendary Edition, I'd recommend you purchase it. If you're a first-time player and a lover of well-written space opera, interesting characters, and RPGs, there's never been a better time to dive into Mass Effect.

The Mass Effect series is to gamers what Star Trek is to movie fans. It is a grandiose space opera that unfolds an epic story about saving the galaxy on the surface of three RPG games.
Thanks to the incredible scope of the scenario, you will get to know the fictional universe and its inhabitants in unprecedented depth.

I will try to describe the core and atmosphere of the series without major spoilers.
As the commander of a unique spaceship and special strike force, you travel the galaxy to intervene where needed and make many difficult choices that you then have to live with. While you get to know the individual alien races and assemble your party, a very successfully dosed central plot slowly begins to develop in the background, revolving around the suspiciously similar mythology of many space civilizations - ancient records tell of a divine race of thinking machines that return in cycles to "harvest" organic life.

One of the main charms of Mass Effect lies in the gradual and slow unraveling of the complex relationships between the many cosmic races, blindly chasing the main goal while trying to tick off another completed game is completely counterproductive.

It is fascinating to observe from a distance how well all three parts of the game work even after all these years and fit perfectly into the mosaic of a single, perfectly connected story. It is in this interconnectedness that the great strength of the Legendary Edition as a package lies, as it offers an easy way to enjoy all the content of the main games as well as their often excellent or even absolutely essential DLC additions, which have been organically integrated directly into the main games for this edition. And although a great progress can be felt between the individual parts not only in terms of the setting or gameplay, but also in terms of storytelling, a certain naivety and old worldliness of the first part is suitably contrasted with the captivating personal level of the second part, so that everything culminates in an absolute war epic in the final three.

Epic soundtracks, an interesting and unique universe, one of the best stories in the gaming industry... there is nothing to think about, going through this trilogy is the duty of every gamer. [b] 95% [/b]

[h1] Mass Effect 1 [/h1]

[b] Pros: [/b]
- Amazing main storyline
- Great cast of characters
- Strong writing
- Incredibly engaging worldbuilding
- Decent RPG mechanics and progression
- Pretty good soundtrack

[b] Cons: [/b]
- Very lackluster combat that doesn't feel very good
- Tedious hacking minigame
- Tedious collectahon side quests
- Incredibly dull level design. Very repetitive, often baren and copy + paste
- Too many interiors look like obvious combat arenas which feel out of place and breaks immersion
- Lackluster exploration and Mako (vehicle) gameplay feels very sloppy and sluggish
- Paragon and Renegade system feels a bit restrictive, in that it rewards you for sticking to one throughout an entire playthrough, limiting player freedom

[b] Final Verdict [/b]
- A solid 8/10 game. Great introduction to the Mass Effect universe and some of its central themes and characters.

[h1] Mass Effect 2 [/h1]

[b] Pros: [/b]
- Incredibly compelling characters and character storylines
- Some of the best writing in any RPG ever
- Highly improved combat compared to ME1. Actually feels good to play now
- One of the best if not THE BEST final mission/level in any roleplaying game ever made
- Companions Companions Companions
- Fleshed out worldbuilding, with more variety in aliens, politics, religion, philosophy, art, world design and locations
- Incredible soundtrack with many memorable tracks as well as returning favorites from ME1
- Actual consequences for a variety of your decisions throughout the game
- Paragon and Renegade conversation interupts are a great addition that keeps conversations engaging and interactive

[b] Cons: [/b]
- Next to no exploration this time around. Limited to exploring hub zones
- Streamlined ability trees and progression which makes balancing easier but limits the amount of choice and variety
- Paragon and Renegade system suffers from the same problems as in ME1
- The new hacking minigames offer some variety from ME1, however they quickly turn just as tedious and boring
- Weapon restrictions on classes once again limits player choice
- Probing planets for essential resources is one of the most dull and mind numbing activities in the entire trilogy

[b] Final Verdict [/b]
- An easy 9.5/10. One of the best RPGs ever made and a huge improvement on almost all aspects over ME1. Some elements like exploration and deeper gear/character progression being scrapped doesn't hurt the overall experience, but it does limit the game's actual potential of hitting a 10/10.

[h1] Mass Effect 3 [/h1]

[b] Pros: [/b]
- The best combat gameplay in the trilogy. Feels incredibly smooth and fun to play
- Lots of weapons, abilities and builds to experiment with. Easily the best in the trilogy
- Has some of best story moments in the entire trilogy. Ironically also has some of the lowest
- Is able to reap what has been sowed in the previous two games for MASSIVE benefits
- Relationships, character bonding and moments are as strong as they have ever been
- Paragon and Renegade system has finally been fixed, with both styles contributing to one reputation bar that will unlock more dialogue options for both styles instead of forcing you to stick with only one
- Characters move around the Normandy in-between missions which opens up for a huge variety of character interactions. Unfortunately, they are also easily missable
- Comes with a new map for tracking companions, important NPCs and the like
- The Shoreleave Citadel content is some of the funniest stuff I have ever played. Pure fanservice, but done in an intelligent and respectable manner that doesn't take away from the core experience
- Once again an amazing soundtrack that sounds quite different than the music in the previous two games, however it fits just as well because of the circumstances

[b] Cons: [/b]
- The removal of the neutral dialogue option is a baffling choice that severely hurts dialogue
- Again almost no exploration whatsoever
- Kai Leng
- The story gets quite convoluted with some its explanations towards the end and things become hard to believe
- The "nightmare" sequences that Shepard has feel forced because of what they focus on. Had they focused on prior decisions made in the previous games, they would have been more effective and dynamic
- War Assets are unfortunately not as impactful as upgrades and squad loyalty were in ME2 and ultimately only boils down to what endings are available rather than a plethora of different outcomes and scenes/interactions
- The ending itself can feel very contrived and ultimately not at all satisfactory regardless of the Galaxy or Shepard's fate

[b] Final Verdict [/b]
- Still a solid 9/10 game. The game does fall flat on its face here and there, but with the improvements to the gameplay, the character interactions while also having some of the best moments in the entire trilogy still makes this a worthwhile game to play through.

I bought this on June 1, just finished my first three game play through on June 8. 

I didn't even know 7 days passed.

Absolutely awesome! 

As a long-time Mass Effect fan, I'm in heaven. ^^ 
The graphic update (especially for ME1) is incredible. 
The clipping errors (mostly ME2) are gone. The Illusive Man's finger is no longer clipping through the cigarette in the Intro, Udina's eyes stopped glitching. Shepard's fingers remain on her earpice (whenever she's talking with the Normandy) where they abruptly changed position in the original game, moving up and down from one closeup to the next. 
Same goes for Lorik Qui'in's eyes in ME1 (glitching like Udina's), Saren's claws (clipping) when gripping Benethia's jaw. 
The Peak 15/Ilos black bug is gone. And the random freezing/crashes on the Citadel (whenever one had to go through opening doors) are also gone. 

The DLC-integration is flawless, and I'm definitely not sad that Pinnacle Station is no longer part of the trilogy. 

The modding abilities are insane. Thanks to the series being 100 % Single-Player now, installing mods is now incredibly easy. 

All in all, paying 60 Euros for three games + all their DLCs is quite the bargain per se - unless you're a cheapskate like me, lol. i waited until the Black Friday deal and got the Legendary Edition for 35 Euros.

I paused before writing this review. Unsure how to express my feelings and do this game justice. 
I know this an impossible task, but I am inspired to try and so here we go.

      If you haven't played this series before, you are very lucky. You get to experience it for the first time. 
Make it count. If anyone ever asks you why video games are a form of art, this is the game you need to show them. Bioware knew what you wanted from a perfect videogame, and they gave it to you....
And then they kept going and gave you more than you could have expected. It couldn't be anything less than a passion project. 

     You won't merely make moral decisions. 
You will be forced to commit to them. You will be forced to take responsibility. They will test your resolve, make you doubt them long after they have been made. Effect the world around you and the characters around you and your reputation on a widespread scale of immense detail. They will challenge your sense of morality and make you look at real life, other people, and the decisions we make in a different light. From a perspective you never considered. When you are done you will be a more confident decision maker in real life.

       You won't merely like the characters.
You will bond with your squad. You will be driven by their motivations. You will stress when tensions rise. You will suffer with their losses and cheer with their victories. You will come to think of them as your real friends because they are distinct and convincing. You will fall in love with them. You will feel responsible for their lives in your hands. When someone threatens them your blood will boil, and when they come to your defense you won't be able to help but grin. Most importantly, you will miss them when it's all over. 

         You won't merely be immersed in the story.
You will remember it for the rest of your life as if you were there. The Reapers will haunt your dreams. You will have experiences that become key memories. You will become a wiser, more intelligent, more philosophical person. You will feel like you are doing something important and life's problems won't matter for a while. The real test will come when least expected - turning everything upside down with game mechanics hidden behind the scenes that I've never seen before in a video game. 

And then it will all be over ... and you will sit and contemplate the decisions you made. The outcome you forged with your own hands. You will look at your life differently, now a more mature person than when you started. You will be sad that you will never have that experience for the first time again, and you will realize that it's quite possible you will never be entertained so greatly again. 

So board your space ship, lead your crew, grab your weaponry and choose your biotic powers. Uncover the dark wonders and cosmic horrors that await you in deep space. The Universe and its life forms are counting on you. But don't worry, you got this. After all, you're Commander Shepard, survivor of the N7 training program. And your crew is the best at what they do. 

This is a uncut diamond that goes on sale for $5 just because it is somewhat old now. This is the quality blueprint from which to judge all others. A perfect videogame.

Born too late to explore Earth
Born too soon to explore Space
Born just in time to explore Mass Effect
